title: Honi and the Carob Tree, Akiva and the Water
bigQuestion: What can a tree and a drip of water teach about learning and giving?

story.title: A Tree for Someone Else
story.kicker: An old man plants a tree he will never eat from, and a passerby cannot understand why.
paragraphs: One day a man named Honi was walking down a road. He saw an old man digging a hole. The old man put a small tree in the hole. It was a carob tree. Honi stopped to watch.
Honi asked a question. "How long until this tree gives fruit?" The old man said, "Seventy years." Honi was surprised. Seventy years is a very long time. The old man would not live that long.

"Then why plant it?" Honi asked. "You will never eat from it." The old man smiled. He said, "When I was born, there were carob trees. My grandparents planted them for me. So I plant this tree for my grandchildren."
Honi sat down to think about that. The Talmud says he fell asleep. And the story gets even stranger. But that part is for the next lesson.
story.think: Have you ever done something nice for a person you will never meet? What was it?

lessons.title: A Man Plants a Tree
lessons.mainIdea: The Talmud tells how Honi met an old man planting a carob tree for his grandchildren.
reading: *Honi* was a Jewish teacher. He lived about 2,000 years ago in the land of Israel. Jewish tradition remembers him for praying for rain. The Talmud tells stories about him.
In one story, Honi saw an old man plant a *carob* tree. A carob tree grows sweet brown pods. But it takes a long time to grow. The old man said: seventy years.
Honi asked why plant it. The old man said his grandparents planted trees for him. So he would plant for his grandchildren. He was planting for people not born yet.

words.d: a Jewish teacher from about 2,000 years ago; the Talmud tells how he met a man planting a carob tree
a tree that grows sweet brown pods; the Talmud says it takes seventy years to give fruit

look.title: The Talmud Tells It
look.text: The Talmud says Honi saw a man planting a carob tree and asked how many years until it would bear fruit. The man said seventy years. Honi asked if he was sure he would live seventy years. The man answered that he found carob trees in the world when he was born; as his ancestors planted for him, he was planting for his descendants.
look.cite: Babylonian Talmud, Ta'anit 23a, retold in simple words (compare Rodkinson's translation, 1896–1903)
look.prompt: Who did the old man say planted trees for him?

check.q: What kind of tree did the old man plant?
check.why: The Talmud says the old man planted a carob tree.

check.q: How long did the old man say the tree would take?
check.why: The old man said the carob tree would give fruit in seventy years.

check.q: Who was the old man planting the tree for?
check.why: He said he was planting for his grandchildren, as his grandparents had planted for him.

lessons.title: Seventy Years
lessons.mainIdea: In the Talmud's story, Honi sleeps seventy years and wakes to see the tree giving fruit.
reading: The story goes on. Honi sat down to eat. He fell asleep. Rocks hid him from sight. The Talmud says he slept for *seventy* years!
When Honi woke up, he saw a man picking carobs. It was the same tree. Honi asked, "Did you plant this?" The man said, "No. My grandfather did."
The old man's plan had worked. His grandchild was eating the fruit. Jewish tradition tells this story to teach about giving to the future.

words.d: the number 70; in the story, how long a carob tree takes and how long Honi slept

look.title: Numbers in the Stories
rows: Years for the carob tree to give fruit
Years Honi slept in the story
Akiva's age when he started to learn
Years Akiva studied away from home
look.cite: Babylonian Talmud, Ta'anit 23a; Ketubot 62b–63a; Avot de-Rabbi Natan, chapter 6
look.prompt: Which two numbers are the same? Why do you think the story uses the same number twice?

check.q: What happened to Honi after he sat down?
check.why: The Talmud says Honi fell asleep and slept for seventy years.

check.q: Who was picking carobs when Honi woke up?
check.why: The man said his grandfather had planted the tree. He was the grandchild.

check.q: What does Jewish tradition use this story to teach?
check.why: The story is told to teach about planting for people who come after us.

lessons.title: The Shepherd
lessons.mainIdea: Rabbi Akiva started as a shepherd who could not read, and he began to learn as a grown-up.
reading: Rabbi *Akiva* became one of the most famous rabbis in the Talmud. But he did not start as a rabbi. He started as a *shepherd*. A shepherd takes care of sheep.
Akiva was poor. He could not read. He worked for a rich man. The Talmud says the rich man's daughter saw that Akiva was good and humble. She married him.
She told Akiva to go and study. Jewish tradition says he was about forty years old. He had to learn the alphabet, like a small child. He did it anyway.

words.d: a famous rabbi in the Talmud who began as a shepherd and started learning as a grown-up
a person who takes care of sheep

look.title: Starting Late
look.text: Look at a grown man sitting on a small bench. Around him are little children. They are all learning the alphabet. The man is much older than everyone else. He holds his slate and says the letters out loud, one by one. He does not look ashamed. He looks like he wants to learn.
look.prompt: How might Akiva have felt learning with little children? What might have helped him keep going?

check.why: The Talmud says Akiva was a shepherd before he learned to read.

check.q: About how old was Akiva when he began to learn?
check.why: Jewish tradition says Akiva was about forty when he began to study.

check.q: Who told Akiva to go and study?
check.why: The Talmud says his wife told him to go and learn Torah.

lessons.title: Water and Stone
lessons.mainIdea: Akiva saw water wearing a hole in a stone and decided learning could shape him too.
reading: Jewish tradition tells how Akiva got the courage to learn. One day he stood by a well. He saw a stone with a hole in it. Water dripped on the stone.
Akiva asked, "Who made this hole?" People said the water did. It fell drip by drip, day after day. Slowly, it wore a hole in the hard stone.
Akiva thought about that. Water is soft. Stone is hard. But water won. He said: if water can shape stone, then learning can shape me. He began to *study*.

words.d: to spend time learning something, a little at a time

look.title: The Drip That Won
look.text: An old rabbinic book tells that Akiva, at forty years old, had not yet learned anything. He stood by a well and saw a stone worn away. He asked who had hollowed it out, and was told the water had done it, drop by drop. He said to himself: if soft water can carve hard stone, then words of Torah, which are hard, can surely carve my heart, which is flesh.
look.cite: Avot de-Rabbi Natan, chapter 6, retold in simple words
look.prompt: What did Akiva decide when he saw the hole in the stone?

check.q: What made the hole in the stone?
check.why: The water dripped on the stone day after day and wore a hole in it.

choices: Learning could shape him, a little at a time.
He was too old to learn.
check.why: Akiva said that if water can shape stone, learning can shape him.

check.q: Which book tells the water and stone story?
check.why: The story is in Avot de-Rabbi Natan, an old rabbinic book, chapter 6.

lessons.title: Planting for Others
lessons.mainIdea: The carob tree story teaches about giving to people who will come after us.
reading: Think about the old man again. He worked hard. He dug a hole and planted a tree. He knew he would never taste the fruit. He did it anyway.
Jewish tradition calls this kind of giving a gift to the *future*. The future is the time that has not come yet. You can help people you will never meet.
Kids can plant for the future too. You can plant a real tree. You can leave a room clean for the next class. You can teach a younger kid a game.

words.d: the time that has not come yet; tomorrow, next year, and long after

look.title: A Gift You Will Not See
look.text: Look at a class planting little trees on the edge of a playground in Chicago. The trees are only as tall as the kids. In many years, they will be tall and shady. The kids who planted them will be grown up and gone. New kids will sit in the shade.
look.prompt: What is one thing you could do this week for someone who comes after you?

choices: the time that has not come yet
check.why: The future is the time that has not come yet.

check.q: Why is the old man's tree a gift to the future?
choices: Other people will eat the fruit after him.
The tree grew in one day.
check.why: The old man planted so that his grandchildren would eat from the tree.

check.q: Which is a way a kid can plant for the future?
choices: leaving a room clean for the next class
check.why: Leaving a room clean helps the people who come after you.

lessons.title: Never Too Late
lessons.mainIdea: Akiva's story teaches that it is never too late to learn, and that small steps add up.
reading: Akiva began learning at about forty. The Talmud says he studied for many years. He became a great rabbi. Many students came to learn from him.
The Talmud tells stories of the rabbis to teach. Akiva's story teaches two things. It is *never too late* to learn. And little steps add up, like drips of water.
The Talmud is full of rabbis like Hillel, Honi, and Akiva. Their stories are still told today. In this course, you will meet many more of them.

words.d: you can always start; a person can learn at any age

look.title: Two Stories, One Idea
look.text: Story one: an old man plants a tree for seventy years from now. Story two: a grown man learns his letters, one drip at a time. In both stories, something big happens slowly. In both, a person keeps going without seeing the end.
look.prompt: What do the two stories have in common? What is different?

choices: It is never too late to learn.
check.why: Jewish tradition tells Akiva's story to show that learning can start at any age.

choices: a great rabbi with many students
check.why: The Talmud says Akiva became a great rabbi with many students.

check.q: How do little steps in learning work, like the water?
check.why: Like drips of water on stone, small steps in learning add up over time.

review.q: Who saw an old man planting a carob tree?
review.why: The Talmud, in Ta'anit 23a, says Honi saw the old man planting the tree.

review.q: Why did the old man plant a tree he would never eat from?
choices: He was planting for his grandchildren.
He did not know it was slow.
review.why: He said his grandparents planted for him, so he planted for his grandchildren.

review.q: How long did the Talmud say Honi slept?
review.why: In the story Honi sleeps seventy years and wakes to see the tree giving fruit.

review.q: What was Akiva before he was a rabbi?

review.why: The Talmud says Akiva was a poor shepherd who had not learned to read.

review.q: What did Akiva see that made him want to learn?
choices: water wearing a hole in a stone
review.why: Akiva saw water dripping on a stone and decided learning could shape him.

review.q: Which story tells that it is never too late to learn?
review.why: Akiva began learning at about forty and became a great rabbi.
